title: They didn’t just dislike Joseph.
paragraphs: They didn’t just dislike Joseph.
They hated him.

Not because he stole from them.
Not because he lied to them.
Not because he harmed them.
They hated him for something far more dangerous.
A dream.

A dream that did not come from ambition.
A dream that did not come from ego.
A dream that came from God.
Genesis 37 tells us something uncomfortable about the human heart: sometimes the moment God places favor on someone’s life, jealousy wakes up in the room.

Joseph was the young son of Jacob. Seventeen years old. Still growing. Still learning how to carry the weight of revelation. And his father gave him a robe that screamed what everyone already felt—Joseph was loved differently.
The robe was visible.
But the dream?
The dream was explosive.
Joseph dreamed of sheaves in the field bowing down to his sheaf. Later he dreamed of the sun, moon, and eleven stars bowing down before him.
It was not a random dream.
It was prophetic.
And when Joseph shared it… the room turned cold.
Scripture says plainly:

“And his brothers hated him even more for his dreams and his words.”
— Genesis 37:8

Jealousy does not need evidence.
It only needs comparison.
And comparison quickly becomes resentment.
The brothers began to look at Joseph and see something unbearable: God’s hand on his life.
They could not silence the dream.
So they decided to silence the dreamer.
Let that sink in.
Sometimes the people who know your name the longest struggle the most with your calling.
Joseph’s brothers did not see destiny.
They saw competition.
They did not see God’s plan.
They saw a threat.
So hatred started whispering inside their hearts. And hatred, if left alone, eventually becomes action.

First came the mockery.
Then the distance.
Then the conspiracy.
One day Joseph was simply obeying his father—walking across the fields to check on his brothers.
From a distance they saw him coming.
And instead of saying, “Here comes our brother,” they said something chilling:
“Here comes this dreamer.” (Genesis 37:19)
Not Joseph.
The dreamer.
His identity had already been reduced to the thing they despised.
Jealousy will always try to rewrite someone’s identity.
And in that moment they plotted something dark.
“Come now, let’s kill him and throw him into one of these cisterns…” (Genesis 37:20)
All because of a dream.
Think about that.
A teenager with a God-given vision nearly lost his life because envy had grown unchecked.
But here is where the story begins to whisper something deeper.
Joseph’s brothers thought they were ending the dream.
But God was only beginning the journey.
They stripped him of the robe.
They threw him into a pit.
Eventually they sold him into slavery.
If you stopped the story there, it would look like the dream failed.
It would look like jealousy won.
It would look like God’s promise collapsed under human cruelty.
But Scripture reveals something stronger than hatred.
Providence.
What the brothers meant as destruction, God was weaving into deliverance.
The pit was not the end.
It was the doorway.
Years later, Joseph would rise from slavery to become the governor of Egypt. The same brothers who betrayed him would one day stand before him in desperation during famine.
And the dream they hated?
It would come true.
But Joseph’s story does not end with revenge.
It ends with grace.
Joseph looked at the very men who sold him and spoke one of the most powerful lines in the entire Bible:

“You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good…”
— Genesis 50:20
That is the miracle of God’s sovereignty.
People can hate the dream.
They cannot stop the Author of the dream.
But the story of Joseph is also pointing us to Someone greater.
Another beloved Son.
Another rejected one.
Another man betrayed by those close to Him.
Jesus Christ.

Like Joseph, Jesus was hated without cause.
Like Joseph, He was betrayed for silver.
Like Joseph, He was stripped and handed over to suffering.
But through the rejection of Christ, God accomplished the greatest rescue in human history.
The cross looked like defeat.
But it was redemption.
Joseph saved nations from famine.
Jesus saves souls from sin.
And here is the question this story quietly asks every one of us:
What do you do when someone else carries a dream from God?
Do you celebrate it?
Or do you resent it?
Jealousy is a dangerous fire. It burns relationships, distorts identity, and blinds hearts to the goodness of God.
But the Gospel offers a better way.
Instead of competing with others, Christ invites us to surrender to Him.
Because the greatest dream is not fame.
Not power.
Not recognition.
The greatest dream is redemption.
And that dream is available to every person through Jesus.
Maybe someone mocked what God placed in your heart.
Maybe people misunderstood your obedience.
Maybe the road you’re walking feels like a pit instead of a promise.
Listen carefully.
God is not finished writing your story.
The pit is not proof that the dream died.
Sometimes the pit is simply where God prepares the dreamer.

Stay humble.
Stay faithful.
Stay close to Christ.
Because what God begins, no hatred can cancel.
And what God promises, no pit can bury.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
🔥 ENGAGEMENT QUESTION
Have you ever experienced jealousy or rejection because of something God placed in your heart?

People may hate the dream.
But they cannot stop God.
